  • Confirm gestational age > 14 weeks
  • Verify informed consent obtained
  • Empty bladder before procedure
  • Position supine with right-hip wedge
  • Monitor maternal vital signs and FHR throughout and after
  • Always check Rh status — give RhoGAM if Rh-negative
  • Teach red-flag symptoms requiring follow-up
  • Document procedure tolerance, fluid obtained, results pending
Worked Example Newborn Screening Tests Ch 24 — Nursing Care of Newborns
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure Name
Newborn Screening Tests
Review Module Chapter
Ch 24 — Nursing Care of Newborns

Description of Procedure

Universal screening of all newborns for genetic, metabolic, hormonal, and cardiac disorders that, if undetected, can cause significant morbidity or death. Required by all 50 US states (specific panels vary). Performed before hospital discharge, typically at 24-48 hours of life.

Indications

  • All newborns — universal screening regardless of risk
  • Detection of treatable conditions in asymptomatic newborns
  • Conditions screened may include > 30 disorders depending on state

Interpretation of Findings

  • Metabolic screen: abnormal or inadequate samples require repeat and/or confirmatory diagnostic testing; a positive screen is not a diagnosis.
  • Hearing screen: result is pass or refer; refer requires repeat screening and audiology follow-up if persistent.
  • CCHD screen: pass if SpO₂ is ≥ 95% in the right hand and foot and the difference is ≤ 3%; failed screen requires provider evaluation and often echocardiogram.
  • Bilirubin screen: TcB/serum bilirubin is plotted by age in hours to determine risk zone and need for repeat testing or treatment.
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-procedure:

  • Educate parents about each screening test and rationale.
  • Obtain consent or document informed refusal according to policy.
  • Verify newborn has been feeding for 24+ hours when needed for metabolic-screen accuracy.
  • Gather supplies: heel warmer, alcohol pads, lancet, filter paper card, gauze, and bandage.

Intra-procedure:

  • For metabolic screening, warm the heel, use the lateral aspect, cleanse and dry skin, wipe away the first drop, fill all filter-paper circles, and avoid squeezing or touching circles.
  • For hearing screening, perform OAE or ABR in a quiet environment with the newborn sleeping.
  • For CCHD screening, place pulse oximeter on the right hand and either foot at ≥ 24 hours of life.
  • For bilirubin screening, obtain TcB or serum bilirubin before discharge and plot results by age in hours.

Post-procedure:

  • Apply pressure to heel-stick site, comfort newborn with sucrose/breastfeeding/swaddling, and document time, site, sample appearance, and tolerance.
  • Send metabolic screen to the state lab and communicate immediate hearing/CCHD results.
  • Arrange repeat testing or referral for abnormal, refer, failed, or inadequate results.

Client Education

  • Metabolic screening checks for treatable disorders such as PKU, congenital hypothyroidism, galactosemia, sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, SCID, and MCAD deficiency.
  • Hearing screening helps identify hearing loss early for intervention.
  • CCHD screening detects critical heart defects before symptoms become life-threatening.
  • Bilirubin screening identifies newborns at risk for severe hyperbilirubinemia.
  • Metabolic results usually return in 1-2 weeks; hearing and CCHD results are immediate.
  • If a screen is positive, it means confirmatory testing is needed, not that the newborn has a confirmed diagnosis.
  • Schedule the first newborn visit at 3-5 days after discharge and keep all repeat-screening appointments.

Potential Complications

  • Heel bruising or bleeding (minor)
  • Newborn discomfort during procedure
  • False positives (more common than false negatives)
  • False negatives if test done before 24 hr of feeds
  • Parental anxiety during waiting period
  • Need for repeat testing if inadequate sample
  • Cellulitis or osteomyelitis if improper heel stick technique (very rare)

Nursing Interventions

  • Perform required metabolic, hearing, CCHD, and bilirubin screens before discharge according to timing requirements.
  • Use safe heel-stick technique on the lateral heel and comfort the newborn during/after specimen collection.
  • Document screening results, sample quality, newborn tolerance, parent teaching, and any refusal.
  • Notify pediatrician/neonatologist of abnormal or failed screens and arrange repeat testing or referrals.
  • Coordinate follow-up with audiology, pediatric cardiology, genetics, endocrinology, hematology, pulmonology, public health, or social work as indicated.
Worked Example Contraction Stress Test (CST) Ch 6 — Assessment of Fetal Well-Being
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure Name
Contraction Stress Test (CST)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 6 — Assessment of Fetal Well-Being

Description of Procedure

Test to assess fetal response to uterine contractions — evaluates uteroplacental function. Contractions stress the placenta — if fetus is well-oxygenated, no late decelerations. Used in high-risk pregnancies or after non-reactive NST. Less commonly performed today (BPP and Doppler often preferred). Two types: spontaneous (using natural contractions) or induced (using IV oxytocin or nipple stimulation).

Indications

  • Non-reactive NST that requires further evaluation
  • Suspected uteroplacental insufficiency
  • Decreased fetal movement
  • IUGR
  • Postdates pregnancy
  • Maternal chronic disease (diabetes, hypertension)
  • Decreased fluid (oligohydramnios)
  • Sometimes used in late preterm/term for high-risk surveillance

Contraindications:

  • Preterm labor risk (contractions could induce labor)
  • Placenta previa
  • Prior classical cesarean (uterine rupture risk)
  • Multiple cesareans
  • Prior uterine rupture
  • PPROM
  • Multiple gestation

Interpretation of Findings

Goal: Three contractions of moderate intensity, lasting 40-60 seconds, in 10-minute window.

Results:

  • Negative (NORMAL/REASSURING): NO late decelerations with contractions; placenta functioning well; suggests fetal well-being
  • Positive (ABNORMAL): Late decelerations with > 50% of contractions; suggests uteroplacental insufficiency; may need delivery
  • Equivocal-suspicious: intermittent late decels or significant variables; needs repeat or additional testing
  • Equivocal-hyperstimulatory: late decels with contractions every 2 min or lasting > 90 sec
  • Unsatisfactory: inadequate contractions or uninterpretable tracing
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-procedure:

  • Verify gestational age (typically > 32-34 weeks)
  • Check for contraindications
  • Informed consent
  • Patient empties bladder
  • Side-lying position (avoid supine hypotension)
  • Baseline vital signs, FHR baseline
  • External fetal monitor (tocodynamometer + FHR)
  • Establish IV access (if oxytocin will be used)

Intra-procedure:

  • Nipple stimulation method: warm cloth over one nipple, massage for 2 min; rest; repeat as needed
  • Oxytocin method: begin at 0.5-1 mU/min IV, double every 15-20 min until adequate contraction pattern (max 10 mU/min)
  • Monitor FHR continuously
  • Monitor maternal vital signs Q15 min
  • Watch for hyperstimulation (contractions every < 2 min or lasting > 90 seconds)
  • Stop stimulation if adequate pattern achieved or for hyperstim

Post-procedure:

  • Continue monitoring until contractions subside
  • Vital signs
  • Discharge planning based on results
  • If positive: prepare for further evaluation/delivery

Client Education

  • Procedure takes 1-2 hours
  • Monitors will be on belly
  • Goal is to have a few contractions
  • You'll feel mild to moderate cramping
  • Nipple stimulation may be used (less invasive) or IV oxytocin
  • Important to lie on your side
  • Tell us if you have severe pain, vaginal bleeding, or fluid leakage
  • Most often results are reassuring
  • If positive — additional testing or delivery may be recommended
  • Don't eat heavy meal beforehand
  • Empty bladder before

Potential Complications

  • Induction of preterm labor (in susceptible patients)
  • Hyperstimulation (excessive contractions) → fetal distress
  • Uterine rupture (especially with prior cesarean)
  • Fetal distress requiring emergent delivery
  • Cord prolapse if membranes rupture during test
  • Maternal hypotension
  • Equivocal results requiring repeat testing
  • Anxiety

Nursing Interventions

  • Pre-procedure: confirm gestational age, check contraindications, IV access, informed consent
  • Side-lying position to prevent supine hypotension
  • Continuous fetal monitoring
  • Vital signs Q15 min
  • Watch for hyperstimulation — stop stimulation if occurs
  • Treat hyperstimulation: terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ
  • Document contraction pattern and FHR response
  • Recognize positive result and notify provider
  • Post: continue monitoring until uterus quiet
  • Educate on results and next steps
  • Discharge with follow-up plan
Worked Example MSAFP and Quad Marker Screening Ch 6 — Assessment of Fetal Well-Being
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure Name
Maternal Serum Alpha-Fetoprotein / Quad Screen
Review Module Chapter
Ch 6 — Assessment of Fetal Well-Being

Description of Procedure

Maternal serum screening for fetal abnormalities. MSAFP (single marker) and the more comprehensive Quad Screen (four markers) detect risk of neural tube defects (NTDs), Down syndrome, and Trisomy 18. Performed at 15-20 weeks gestation (ideally 16-18 weeks). Screening test only — not diagnostic.

Quad markers:

  • AFP (alpha-fetoprotein)
  • hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin)
  • Estriol
  • Inhibin A

Indications

  • Routine offering at 15-20 weeks (ideally 16-18 weeks)
  • All pregnant women offered, regardless of age
  • Especially recommended for: advanced maternal age (35+), family history of genetic disorders, prior child with NTD or chromosomal abnormality, abnormal first-trimester screen
  • Often combined with first-trimester screening as "sequential" or "integrated"

Interpretation of Findings

Reported as risk (e.g., 1 in 100):

  • Results compared with age-adjusted population risk
  • "Positive" or "increased risk" — does NOT mean fetus is affected; just indicates need for further testing
  • "Negative" or "screen negative" — risk lower than threshold, doesn't guarantee normal fetus

Interpretation patterns:

  • ↑ AFP: NTD (spina bifida, anencephaly); abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis, omphalocele); multiple gestation; underestimated gestational age; intrauterine fetal death
  • ↓ AFP: Down syndrome, Trisomy 18, overestimated gestational age
  • Down syndrome pattern: ↓ AFP, ↑ hCG, ↓ estriol, ↑ inhibin A
  • Trisomy 18 pattern: ↓ AFP, ↓ hCG, ↓ estriol, normal/↑ inhibin A

Sensitivity/specificity:

  • Quad screen: ~80% sensitivity for Down syndrome with 5% false positive rate
  • MSAFP alone: ~80% sensitivity for open NTDs
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-procedure:

  • Informed consent — woman should understand it's a screening test, not diagnostic
  • Verify accurate gestational age (critical — gestational age error causes false positives)
  • Documentation of LMP, ultrasound dating
  • Identification confirmed
  • Pre-test counseling on possible results and next steps

Intra-procedure:

  • Simple venipuncture for maternal serum
  • Standard blood draw technique

Post-procedure:

  • Results in 1-2 weeks typically
  • Communicate results to patient
  • If positive screen: offer counseling and additional testing
  • Provide genetic counseling referral
  • Discuss options for confirmatory testing: amniocentesis, detailed ultrasound, NIPT (cell-free DNA)

Client Education

  • Voluntary test — your choice
  • It's a screening test, not diagnostic — tells us the risk, not whether your baby has the condition
  • Positive screen does NOT mean your baby is affected — about 1 in 20 women have positive results but most have normal babies
  • Negative screen doesn't guarantee a normal baby — false negatives possible
  • Detects: spinal cord defects (spina bifida), Down syndrome, Trisomy 18
  • Requires accurate dating — your provider may do ultrasound to confirm gestational age
  • Performed at 15-20 weeks, ideal 16-18
  • Simple blood test, results in 1-2 weeks
  • If positive: additional testing options will be discussed (detailed ultrasound, amniocentesis, NIPT) — your decision
  • Genetic counseling available
  • Decisions about what to do with results are yours to make

Potential Complications

  • False positive results causing anxiety
  • Maternal anxiety waiting for results
  • Decisions about further invasive testing
  • Limited sensitivity — misses some affected fetuses
  • Confused interpretation if gestational age inaccurate
  • Multiple gestation may alter results
  • Maternal diabetes affects AFP
  • Decisions about continuing pregnancy if confirmed abnormal
  • Ethical considerations

Nursing Interventions

  • Educate that screening is optional
  • Provide accurate, balanced information
  • Ensure informed consent
  • Verify accurate dating
  • Coordinate blood draw at appropriate gestational age
  • Document results in chart
  • Communicate results clearly
  • Provide emotional support
  • Refer to genetic counseling if needed
  • Discuss further testing options non-directively
  • Respect patient's decisions
  • Note: newer NIPT (cell-free fetal DNA) is more accurate for chromosomal screening
Worked Example PUBS and CVS Ch 6 — Assessment of Fetal Well-Being
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure Name
Percutaneous Umbilical Blood Sampling (PUBS) and Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 6 — Assessment of Fetal Well-Being

Description of Procedure

Both are invasive diagnostic procedures with small risk of fetal loss.

CVS (Chorionic Villus Sampling):

  • Performed at 10-13 weeks gestation (earlier than amniocentesis)
  • Obtains chorionic villi (placental tissue) for genetic analysis
  • Two approaches: transcervical (catheter through cervix) or transabdominal (needle through abdominal wall)
  • Ultrasound guidance
  • Detects chromosomal abnormalities (Down syndrome, Trisomy 18, etc.) and many genetic disorders
  • Cannot detect NTDs

PUBS (Percutaneous Umbilical Blood Sampling / Cordocentesis):

  • Performed at 18+ weeks gestation
  • Obtains fetal blood from umbilical cord
  • Needle through maternal abdomen → umbilical vein under ultrasound guidance
  • Highest fetal loss rate of any invasive procedure (~1-2%)
  • Used when rapid diagnosis or specific fetal blood test needed

Indications

CVS:

  • Maternal age 35+ years
  • Abnormal first-trimester screen
  • Family history of genetic disorder
  • Parent is known carrier
  • Prior pregnancy with chromosomal abnormality
  • Earlier diagnosis preferred (vs amniocentesis)

PUBS:

  • Rapid chromosomal analysis when needed (severe IUGR, late detection of abnormality)
  • Fetal anemia evaluation (Rh sensitization, parvovirus)
  • Fetal blood transfusions (e.g., for severe hemolytic disease)
  • Fetal blood typing
  • Fetal infection testing (viral PCR)
  • Fetal platelet count (alloimmune thrombocytopenia)

Interpretation of Findings

CVS results:

  • Preliminary chromosomal results: 7-14 days
  • Detects: chromosomal abnormalities, many genetic disorders
  • Cannot detect: NTDs (would require AFP)

PUBS results:

  • Rapid chromosomal analysis (24-48 hours)
  • Fetal hematocrit, platelet count
  • Fetal blood type
  • Specific infection testing
  • Allows simultaneous treatment (transfusion)
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-procedure (both):

  • Detailed informed consent
  • Verify gestational age
  • Genetic counseling prior
  • Rh status: RhoGAM if Rh-negative mother after procedure
  • Empty bladder
  • Ultrasound to locate placenta, fetus
  • Local anesthesia for abdominal approach

CVS intra-procedure:

  • Lithotomy position (transcervical) or supine (transabdominal)
  • Aseptic prep
  • Speculum exam if transcervical
  • Catheter or needle inserted under ultrasound guidance
  • Aspirate small amount of chorionic villi
  • Procedure 15-30 minutes

PUBS intra-procedure:

  • Supine, slight tilt
  • Aseptic prep
  • Continuous ultrasound guidance
  • Needle through abdominal wall → umbilical vein (typically near placental cord insertion)
  • Fetal blood sample drawn (1-4 mL)
  • Possible transfusion if indicated
  • Procedure 30-60 minutes

Post-procedure:

  • Monitor fetal heart rate Q15-30 min × 1 hour
  • Maternal vital signs
  • Watch for cramping, bleeding, ROM
  • RhoGAM administered if Rh-negative
  • Activity restrictions × 24-48 hours (rest, no intercourse, no heavy lifting)
  • Educate on warning signs
  • Discharge instructions
  • Results follow-up

Client Education

  • Both are invasive — small risk of fetal loss
  • CVS: ~0.5-1% loss rate (similar to amniocentesis)
  • PUBS: 1-2% loss rate (highest)
  • Done by experienced specialist (maternal-fetal medicine)
  • Procedure takes 15-60 minutes
  • Some discomfort, cramping
  • Rh-negative women need RhoGAM
  • Rest 24-48 hours after
  • Watch for: vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, severe cramping, fever, decreased fetal movement → call provider
  • Results take days to weeks
  • Most procedures have normal results
  • Decisions about pregnancy based on results are yours
  • Genetic counseling support

Potential Complications

CVS complications:

  • Fetal loss (~0.5-1%)
  • Bleeding
  • Infection (chorioamnionitis)
  • Limb reduction defects (rare, when done < 10 weeks — no longer done that early)
  • Rh sensitization
  • Cramping
  • ROM
  • Anxiety

PUBS complications:

  • Fetal loss (1-2%)
  • Cord hematoma
  • Fetal bradycardia (most resolves)
  • Fetal hemorrhage from puncture site
  • Infection
  • Rh sensitization
  • Premature labor
  • Maternal hematoma

Nursing Interventions

  • Detailed informed consent
  • Verify accurate gestational age
  • Pre-procedure ultrasound
  • Empty bladder
  • IV access
  • Rh status — RhoGAM ready if Rh-negative
  • Aseptic technique
  • Continuous fetal monitoring during procedure
  • Post-procedure FHR monitoring
  • Maternal vital signs
  • Watch for: bleeding, cramping, ROM, fever
  • RhoGAM administration if indicated
  • Discharge instructions: rest, warning signs, when to call
  • Coordinate genetic counseling
  • Communicate results
  • Emotional support
  • Decision-making support
Worked Example Routine Prenatal Laboratory Tests Ch 4 — Prenatal Care
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure Name
Routine Prenatal Laboratory Tests
Review Module Chapter
Ch 4 — Prenatal Care

Description of Procedure

Battery of laboratory tests performed during prenatal care to identify conditions that affect pregnancy outcomes. Tests scheduled at different gestational ages.

First prenatal visit:

  • CBC (anemia, infection)
  • Blood type, Rh, antibody screen
  • Rubella immunity
  • Varicella immunity (history or titer)
  • HIV, syphilis (RPR/VDRL), hepatitis B
  • Hepatitis C (universal recommendation now)
  • Chlamydia, gonorrhea (NAAT)
  • Pap smear (if due)
  • Urinalysis, urine culture
  • TSH (some)
  • Glucose (screening if high-risk)
  • Tuberculosis screening if at risk

10-13 weeks:

  • First-trimester screening: PAPP-A + hCG + nuchal translucency (NT)
  • Cell-free fetal DNA (NIPT) — optional

15-20 weeks:

  • Quad screen or single AFP

24-28 weeks:

  • GDM screening: 1-hour 50g glucose challenge → 3-hour 100g if abnormal
  • Repeat CBC, antibody screen (if Rh-negative)
  • RhoGAM at 28 weeks if Rh-negative
  • Repeat HIV, syphilis (some)

35-37 weeks:

  • GBS culture
  • HIV, syphilis re-testing

Third trimester (high-risk):

  • NSTs, BPP, ultrasound
  • Repeat antibody screen if Rh-negative

Indications

Indications for all pregnant women:

  • Universal screening for routine prenatal labs
  • Identify treatable conditions early
  • Allow for genetic screening
  • Detect infections that affect mother/fetus
  • Optimize maternal health

High-risk additional testing:

  • Previous GDM → early glucose screening
  • Anemia → iron studies
  • Sickle cell trait → partner testing, genetic counseling
  • Thyroid disease → close monitoring
  • Substance use → urine toxicology
  • Prior cervical insufficiency → cervical length monitoring
  • Recurrent pregnancy loss → thrombophilia workup, anatomic evaluation

Interpretation of Findings

CBC:

  • Anemia: Hgb < 11 g/dL (first/third trimester) or < 10.5 g/dL (second trimester)
  • Treat with iron supplementation

Blood type and Rh:

  • Rh-negative mothers receive RhoGAM at 28 weeks and within 72 hours postpartum if baby Rh+
  • Indirect Coombs if antibody screen positive

Rubella immunity:

  • Non-immune: rubella vaccine after delivery (live virus — not in pregnancy)
  • Educate about avoiding exposure during pregnancy

Varicella immunity:

  • Non-immune: vaccine after delivery; immune globulin if significant exposure

HIV:

  • Positive: antiretroviral therapy to prevent perinatal transmission

Syphilis (RPR):

  • Positive: confirm with FTA-ABS; treat with penicillin G IM

Hepatitis B:

  • HBsAg positive: refer to specialist; newborn HBIG + vaccine at birth

Chlamydia/Gonorrhea:

  • Positive: treat with appropriate antibiotic; treat partner

Glucose:

  • 1-hour 50g challenge: positive if ≥ 130-140 mg/dL → 3-hour 100g
  • 3-hour GTT abnormal: GDM

GBS:

  • Positive: intrapartum penicillin G
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-procedure:

  • Order tests appropriate for gestational age
  • Patient identification
  • Pre-test counseling for genetic tests
  • Informed consent for screening tests
  • Fasting if needed (glucose)
  • Specimen collection containers ready

Intra-procedure:

  • Aseptic technique for blood draw
  • Proper labeling
  • Special considerations: glucose tolerance test (drink solution, draw at specified intervals; patient stays in clinic; no eating/drinking during test)
  • GBS culture: swab vagina and rectum (single swab, vagina then rectum)
  • Urine: clean catch midstream

Post-procedure:

  • Document tests completed
  • Follow-up on results
  • Communicate results to patient
  • Document results in chart
  • Plan follow-up based on results
  • Schedule next visit
  • Address any abnormal findings

Client Education

  • Prenatal labs are recommended part of care
  • Routine tests help us catch conditions early
  • Genetic screening is optional — discuss with provider
  • Some tests require fasting (glucose) — follow instructions
  • If you have an aversion to needles, let staff know
  • Results discussed at next visit (or sooner if urgent)
  • You may need additional testing based on results (don't panic)
  • Bring insurance information
  • Hydrate before blood draw
  • Don't eat/drink during glucose tolerance test
  • Specific symptoms to report: bleeding, severe pain, fever, severe headache, vision changes, decreased fetal movement
  • Communicate with healthcare team throughout

Potential Complications

  • Anxiety about results
  • False positive screening tests
  • Need for additional invasive testing
  • Discovering serious conditions (HIV, syphilis)
  • Decision-making about screening/diagnostic testing
  • Cost concerns
  • Logistical challenges with multiple appointments
  • Discomfort with frequent blood draws

Nursing Interventions

  • Schedule tests at appropriate gestational ages
  • Order tests based on patient risk factors
  • Confidential, sensitive approach to sexual health, HIV testing
  • Provide pre-test counseling
  • Obtain informed consent for screening tests
  • Coordinate blood draws
  • Educate patient on each test
  • Communicate results promptly
  • Refer for additional testing or consultation
  • Document carefully
  • Coordinate with maternal-fetal medicine
  • Address patient anxieties
  • Help with insurance, financial issues
  • Connect to community resources
Worked Example hCG Verification of Pregnancy Ch 3 — Maternal Adaptation in Early Pregnancy
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure Name
Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) Testing
Review Module Chapter
Ch 3 — Maternal Adaptation in Early Pregnancy

Description of Procedure

Quantitative or qualitative measurement of human chorionic gonadotropin — a glycoprotein hormone produced by the trophoblast (and later the placenta) — to confirm pregnancy, monitor early viability, and detect abnormal pregnancy patterns.

Detectable in serum as early as ~6–8 days post-conception (before missed period) and in urine ~1 week later. Expected pattern: doubles every 48–72 hours in early pregnancy, peaks at 8–11 weeks, then declines.

Indications

  • Suspected pregnancy (positive home test, amenorrhea, presumptive signs)
  • Rule out ectopic pregnancy (low or slow-rising hCG with pelvic pain)
  • Monitor early pregnancy viability (serial draws q48 hr)
  • Diagnose / monitor gestational trophoblastic disease (hCG abnormally elevated)
  • Suspected miscarriage (falling hCG)
  • Confirm completion of miscarriage or D&C (hCG should fall to undetectable)

Interpretation of Findings

  • Confirmed pregnancy with expected hCG curve
  • Appropriate doubling every 48–72 hr in early viable IUP
  • Correlated with ultrasound: gestational sac visible at hCG ~1,500–2,000 mIU/mL (transvaginal)
  • Slow-rising, plateauing, falling, or unexpectedly high hCG patterns require provider follow-up for ectopic pregnancy, pregnancy loss, multiple gestation, or gestational trophoblastic disease.
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-procedure:

  • Verify client identity, test type ordered, last menstrual period, symptoms, and medication/supplement history.
  • Teach that urine testing is qualitative, while serum testing can be quantitative and trended.
  • For serial testing, schedule draws about 48 hours apart and use the same lab when possible.

Intra-procedure:

  • Collect urine or serum sample using standard procedure and label accurately.
  • Document timing of specimen collection because trends guide interpretation.

Post-procedure:

  • Correlate quantitative results with symptoms and transvaginal ultrasound when hCG reaches the discriminatory range.
  • Report concerning trends promptly and provide emotional support when viability, ectopic pregnancy, or loss is being evaluated.

Client Education

  • Explain that one hCG value confirms pregnancy risk/status, but serial values show the trend.
  • Teach expected early-pregnancy rise and that abnormal trends need follow-up rather than self-diagnosis.
  • Tell the client to report pelvic pain, shoulder pain, dizziness, syncope, or heavy bleeding immediately.
  • Review that biotin supplements and very early testing can affect some results; follow lab/provider instructions.

Potential Complications

  • False positives — recent miscarriage, hCG-secreting tumor, certain medications (hCG-containing fertility drugs)
  • False negatives — very early pregnancy (test too soon), dilute urine, expired test
  • Slow-rising hCG — suspect ectopic pregnancy
  • Very high hCG — multiple gestation OR gestational trophoblastic disease
  • Falling hCG — miscarriage, ectopic, or fetal demise
  • Test interference: heterophile antibodies; biotin supplements may cause false negatives in some assays

Nursing Interventions

  • Educate client on expected doubling pattern and what abnormal patterns mean
  • Serial draws q48 hr for monitoring early-pregnancy viability — same lab if possible (assay variability)
  • Correlate result with transvaginal ultrasound at hCG > 1,500–2,000 mIU/mL
  • Educate that home urine tests are qualitative only — quantitative requires serum
  • Avoid biotin supplements 8+ hours before testing
  • Provide emotional support — hCG monitoring usually means concern about ectopic, viability, or pregnancy loss
  • Document trends and report concerning patterns to provider promptly
Worked Example Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) Ch 4 (Prenatal Labs) & Ch 9 (Diabetes in Pregnancy) · GDM screening/diagnosis
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure Name
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (1-hr screen & 3-hr diagnostic)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 9 — Diabetes Mellitus in Pregnancy

Description of Procedure

A two-step blood-glucose test for gestational diabetes (GDM):

  • 1-hr glucose screen: non-fasting; drink a 50 g glucola solution, draw blood 1 hr later. A value > 130–140 mg/dL is a positive screen and warrants the diagnostic test.
  • 3-hr OGTT (diagnostic): fasting blood draw, then a 100 g glucose load with draws at 1, 2, and 3 hr.

Indications

  • Routine screening at 24–28 weeks of gestation for all pregnant clients
  • Earlier/repeat screening with risk factors: obesity, prior GDM or macrosomic infant, family history, glycosuria
  • Positive 1-hr screen → proceed to the 3-hr diagnostic test

Interpretation of Findings

1-hr screen: > 130–140 mg/dL = positive (cutoff varies by facility).

3-hr OGTT — typical upper limits:

  • Fasting < 95 mg/dL
  • 1 hr < 180 mg/dL
  • 2 hr < 155 mg/dL
  • 3 hr < 140 mg/dL

Two or more values at/above these limits = diagnosis of GDM.

Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-procedure:

  • Confirm whether the client is having the nonfasting 1-hr screen or fasting 3-hr diagnostic OGTT.
  • For the 3-hr test, verify NPO status after midnight and baseline fasting blood draw.
  • Explain timing, need to remain in the clinic/lab, and restrictions on food, drinks, smoking, and activity during testing.

Intra-procedure:

  • Have the client drink the glucose solution within the required time, usually about 5 minutes.
  • Start timing after the solution is finished and draw samples exactly at ordered intervals.
  • Keep the client seated/resting and monitor for nausea, vomiting, lightheadedness, or hypoglycemia symptoms.

Post-procedure:

  • Label all specimens accurately and document completion/tolerance.
  • If GDM is diagnosed, reinforce follow-up teaching for nutrition, glucose monitoring, and fetal/newborn risks as directed.

Client Education

  • The 1-hr screen does not require fasting; the 3-hr diagnostic OGTT does.
  • Finish the glucose drink as instructed and avoid eating, drinking, smoking, or walking around during the test.
  • Report nausea, vomiting, dizziness, sweating, or feeling faint during the test.
  • If results diagnose GDM, follow-up focuses on diet, glucose monitoring, and medication if targets are not met.

Potential Complications

  • Nausea/vomiting from the concentrated glucose load (may require rescheduling)
  • Lightheadedness/hypoglycemia symptoms during the fasting test
  • Inaccurate results if the client is not truly fasting or does not finish the solution within the time limit

Nursing Interventions

  • Confirm NPO status for the 3-hr test (fasting after midnight); the 1-hr screen does not require fasting
  • Have the client drink the entire solution within ~5 minutes; start timing from completion
  • Keep the client seated and resting; no smoking or further intake during the test
  • Draw samples on time; label accurately
  • If GDM is diagnosed: teach diet/carbohydrate counting, glucose self-monitoring, and that insulin is added if targets are not met (oral agents per provider). Monitor for macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia.
Worked Example Group B Strep (GBS) Screening Culture Ch 8 — Infections · 35–37 wk rectovaginal culture
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure Name
Group B Streptococcus Rectovaginal Culture
Review Module Chapter
Ch 8 — Infections

Description of Procedure

A swab of the lower vagina and rectum cultured for Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Strep). GBS is often part of normal vaginal flora and can be transmitted to the newborn during labor and birth. Universal screening is done at 36–37 weeks (formerly 35–37) of gestation.

Indications

  • Universal prenatal screening at 36–37 weeks for all pregnant clients
  • Identify carriers to guide intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP)
  • Culture may be omitted if GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy or a prior GBS-affected newborn (treat as positive)

Interpretation of Findings

Positive culture = colonization → give IAP in labor.

Treat as positive / give IAP when:

  • Positive GBS culture this pregnancy, or prior infant with GBS disease
  • Unknown status with delivery < 37 weeks
  • Maternal fever ≥ 38°C (100.4°F) in labor
  • ROM ≥ 18 hours
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-procedure:

  • Schedule universal rectovaginal culture at 36-37 weeks unless the client is already treated as GBS-positive.
  • Explain that no speculum is needed and that the culture guides antibiotics in labor.
  • Verify allergy history so intrapartum antibiotic planning is clear if the result is positive.

Intra-procedure:

  • Obtain one swab from the lower vagina, then rectum; label and send promptly.
  • Document specimen collection and pending result in the prenatal record.

Post-procedure:

  • Ensure GBS status is visible for labor admission.
  • For positive or indicated clients, anticipate intrapartum IV antibiotic prophylaxis and newborn monitoring.

Client Education

  • GBS colonization is common and is not a sexually transmitted infection.
  • A positive result means antibiotics are given during labor to reduce newborn infection risk.
  • Tell the care team in labor if the result is positive, unknown, or if there is a penicillin allergy.
  • Seek care promptly for labor, rupture of membranes, fever, or preterm symptoms.

Potential Complications

Untreated GBS colonization can lead to:

  • Neonatal: early-onset sepsis, pneumonia, respiratory distress, and meningitis
  • Maternal: chorioamnionitis, UTI, postpartum endometritis, and sepsis
  • Preterm labor/birth and low birth weight

Nursing Interventions

  • Obtain the swab of the lower vagina then the rectum (no speculum needed); label and send promptly
  • Document GBS status clearly on the prenatal record so it is available in labor
  • For positive/indicated clients, administer IV penicillin G (or cefazolin/clindamycin if penicillin-allergic) at least 4 hr before delivery when possible
  • Monitor the newborn for sepsis signs (temperature instability, poor feeding, respiratory distress)
  • Reassure that GBS colonization is common and not a sexually transmitted infection
Worked Example Kleihauer-Betke Test Ch 7 (Bleeding) & Ch 6 (PUBS) · Detects fetal blood in maternal circulation
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure Name
Kleihauer-Betke (fetomaternal hemorrhage) Test
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Bleeding During Pregnancy

Description of Procedure

A maternal blood test that detects and quantifies fetal red blood cells in the maternal circulation (fetomaternal hemorrhage). Fetal hemoglobin resists acid elution, so fetal cells stain while maternal cells appear as "ghosts" — the proportion of fetal cells estimates the volume of fetal blood that crossed into the mother.

Indications

  • Abruptio placentae or other significant antepartum bleeding
  • Maternal abdominal trauma in pregnancy
  • Rh-negative client with a suspected large fetomaternal bleed (to calculate additional Rho(D) immune globulin)
  • Verify that fetal blood was obtained during PUBS (Ch 6)

Interpretation of Findings

  • Presence of fetal RBCs confirms fetomaternal hemorrhage
  • The percentage of fetal cells estimates the bleed volume and guides how many vials of Rho(D) immune globulin an Rh-negative client needs
  • A larger fetal-cell fraction indicates a greater hemorrhage and higher fetal risk (anemia, hypoxia)
Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-procedure:

  • Verify indication such as abruption, trauma, antepartum bleeding, or Rh-negative status with suspected large fetomaternal hemorrhage.
  • Pair with ordered type and Rh, antibody screen, CBC, and coagulation studies when part of a bleeding workup.
  • Explain that this is a maternal blood draw used to estimate fetal blood exposure.

Intra-procedure:

  • Draw the maternal venous sample, label accurately, and send promptly.
  • Continue maternal assessment and fetal surveillance as ordered because the test does not treat the bleeding source.

Post-procedure:

  • Report results for provider-directed Rho(D) immune globulin dosing in Rh-negative clients.
  • Continue monitoring maternal bleeding and fetal status, and support the client during acute bleeding or trauma evaluation.

Client Education

  • The test checks whether fetal blood entered the maternal circulation.
  • For Rh-negative clients, the result helps determine whether extra Rho(D) immune globulin is needed.
  • Report increased bleeding, abdominal pain, contractions, leakage of fluid, dizziness, or decreased fetal movement immediately.
  • Follow any additional monitoring or ultrasound instructions after trauma or bleeding.

Potential Complications

The test itself is a simple venipuncture (minimal risk). It flags the underlying problem:

  • Significant fetomaternal hemorrhage → fetal anemia, hypoxia, or demise
  • Rh sensitization if an Rh-negative mother is exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood and under-dosed on Rho(D)

Nursing Interventions

  • Draw the maternal venous sample as ordered; label accurately and send promptly
  • Pair with type & Rh, CBC, and coagulation studies in a bleeding workup
  • For Rh-negative clients, anticipate Rho(D) immune globulin dosing based on the result
  • Continue to monitor fetal status (FHR/BPP) and maternal bleeding; the test does not treat the hemorrhage
  • Provide emotional support — it is usually ordered amid acute bleeding or trauma
Worked Example Newborn Bilirubin & Coombs Testing Ch 27 — Newborn Complications · Hyperbilirubinemia workup
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Procedure Name
Serum/Transcutaneous Bilirubin & Direct Coombs Test
Review Module Chapter
Ch 27 — Management of Newborn Complications

Description of Procedure

  • Total serum bilirubin (TSB): blood test quantifying bilirubin; the gold standard for treatment decisions
  • Transcutaneous bilirubin (TcB): noninvasive skin meter for screening
  • Direct Coombs: detects maternal antibody-coated (sensitized) RBCs on the newborn's cells (immune hemolysis)
  • Paired with newborn blood type & Rh and Hgb/Hct to find the cause of jaundice

Indications

  • Visible jaundice (progresses cephalocaudal: face → trunk → extremities)
  • Risk for hemolytic disease: ABO incompatibility (newborn A/B with type O parent) or Rh incompatibility
  • Prematurity, bruising/cephalohematoma, sepsis, or poor feeding
  • Monitoring response during phototherapy

Interpretation of Findings

Physiologic jaundice (benign): appears after 24 hr, peaks ~day 3–5, resolves by ~day 7 (term).

Pathologic jaundice (red flags):

  • Appears before 24 hr of life
  • Persists beyond day 14
  • TSB rises > 0.5 mg/dL/hr

Positive direct Coombs = immune-mediated hemolysis (ABO/Rh) and supports a pathologic cause.

Considerations

Nursing Interventions (pre, intra, post)

Pre-procedure:

  • Assess jaundice in natural light, note age in hours, risk factors, feeding pattern, stooling, and voiding.
  • Verify ordered TcB, TSB, direct Coombs, newborn blood type/Rh, and Hgb/Hct as indicated.
  • Prepare comfort measures for heel stick or venipuncture if serum testing is needed.

Intra-procedure:

  • Obtain TcB/TSB per protocol and plot bilirubin level on the hour-specific nomogram.
  • Collect Coombs/type/Rh/Hgb/Hct specimens accurately when immune hemolysis is suspected.
  • If phototherapy is used, protect eyes, expose skin appropriately, reposition, and monitor temperature/hydration.

Post-procedure:

  • Trend bilirubin response and ensure ordered follow-up checks after discharge.
  • Promote frequent feeding to enhance bilirubin excretion and monitor for dehydration or worsening jaundice.

Client Education

  • Teach that mild physiologic jaundice is common, but early or rapidly rising jaundice needs prompt evaluation.
  • Explain bilirubin testing, Coombs testing, and why repeat levels may be needed after discharge.
  • Encourage feeding 8-12 times per day unless otherwise directed.
  • Call the provider for poor feeding, lethargy, high-pitched cry, worsening yellow color, fewer wet diapers, or fever.

Potential Complications

  • Kernicterus / acute bilirubin encephalopathy — unconjugated bilirubin deposits in the brain, causing permanent neurologic damage
  • Severe hemolysis → anemia
  • Phototherapy side effects: dehydration (sunken fontanels), loose stools, temperature instability

Nursing Interventions

  • Assess jaundice in natural light, blanching the skin over a bony prominence; note time of onset
  • Obtain TcB/TSB per protocol and plot on the hour-specific nomogram; draw Coombs, type/Rh, Hgb/Hct
  • Promote frequent feeding (8–12/day) to enhance bilirubin excretion in stool
  • During phototherapy: eye shields, minimal clothing, reposition, monitor temperature and hydration, watch for dehydration
  • Educate parents that physiologic jaundice is common and treatable; ensure follow-up bilirubin checks
ATI Active Learning Template

Growth and Development

Active · 7 examples
Worked Example Newborn Physical Development Ch 23 — Newborn Assessment
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Developmental Stage
Newborn (birth to 1 month)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 23 — Newborn Assessment
Expected Growth and Development

Physical Development

Growth at birth (term newborn):

  • Weight: 2500–4000 g (5 lb 8 oz – 8 lb 13 oz)
  • Length: 45–55 cm (18–22 in)
  • Head circumference: 32–37 cm
  • Posterior fontanel closes 2–3 mo; anterior open until ~18 mo

Apgar scoring at 1 and 5 min — HR, RR, muscle tone, reflex irritability, color (0–2 each):

  • 0–3 severe distress · 4–6 moderate · 7–10 minimal

Ballard score (within 48 hr) — assesses gestational age via neuromuscular + physical maturity.

Classification: AGA (10–90%ile) · SGA (<10%ile) · LGA (>90%ile) · LBW (≤2500 g).

Cognitive Development

Piaget — Sensorimotor stage (birth): reflexive activity only.

Neuromotor maturity assessed via reflex symmetry:

  • Sucking and rooting — turns head, sucks when cheek stroked (disappears 3–4 mo)
  • Palmar grasp — grasps placed object (lessens by 3–4 mo)
  • Plantar grasp — toes curl when sole touched (to 8 mo)
  • Moro — arms/legs symmetrically extend then abduct, fingers form "C" (to 8 wk)
  • Tonic neck (fencer) — extends arm/leg on side head is turned to (to 3–4 mo)
  • Babinski — toes fan upward when outer sole stroked (to 1 yr)
  • Stepping — steps when held upright on flat surface (to 4 wk)

Absent or asymmetric reflexes may indicate CNS injury, prematurity, or chromosomal abnormality.

Psychosocial Development

Erikson — Trust vs. Mistrust: begins building trust through consistent caregiver response.

Behavioral states (Brazelton):

  • Deep sleep · light sleep · drowsy · quiet alert (best for bonding) · active alert · crying

Sensory:

  • Vision 8–10 inches; tracks faces; prefers black-white contrast
  • Hearing intact at birth (mature)
  • Distinguishes parent's voice within days

Bonding/attachment — promote early skin-to-skin contact; rooming-in; eye contact during feeds.

Age-Appropriate Activities

No play in the traditional sense — newborns engage through sensory experience and caregiver interaction.

Developmentally appropriate experiences:

  • Skin-to-skin contact (kangaroo care) — regulates temp, glucose, HR; promotes bonding
  • Holding, rocking, swaddling
  • Soft talking, singing
  • Black/white high-contrast images at 8–10 in
  • Mobile (in line of sight)
  • Brief tummy time when awake and observed
  • Breastfeeding/feeding cues honored

Health Promotion

  • Newborn screening (blood spot 24–48 hr, hearing, pulse ox for CCHD) before discharge
  • Establish feeding — breast (first hour skin-to-skin) or iron-fortified formula; vitamin K + erythromycin eye ointment + HepB at birth
  • Safe sleep (SIDS prevention): "back to sleep," firm mattress, no soft bedding, room-share without bed-share
  • Bonding promotion: skin-to-skin, eye contact during feeds, responsive caregiving
  • Parent education on warning signs: jaundice, feeding intolerance, temp instability, lethargy
  • First well-visit within 3–5 days of discharge

Immunizations

Birth (before discharge):

  • Hepatitis B #1 — within 24 hr of birth
  • Vitamin K IM (not technically an immunization but standard at birth — prevents hemorrhagic disease)
  • Erythromycin ophthalmic ointment — prophylaxis for gonococcal/chlamydial conjunctivitis

HepB #2 at 1–2 mo; #3 at 6–18 mo.

If mother is HBsAg+: also give HBIG within 12 hr.

Health Screening

  • Newborn screen (blood spot) 24–48 hr after birth — PKU, congenital hypothyroidism, sickle cell, CF, MCAD, others (state-specific panel)
  • Hearing screening before discharge (OAE or AABR)
  • Pulse oximetry at 24 hr — screen for critical congenital heart disease
  • Bilirubin assessment (visual + transcutaneous; serum if needed)
  • Glucose screening if at-risk (IDM, SGA, LGA, late preterm)
  • Vital signs and weight documented
  • First well-visit within 3–5 days of discharge

Nutrition

Feeding cues: rooting, hand-to-mouth, smacking lips; crying is a LATE sign.

Breastfeeding:

  • Initiate within first hour
  • 8–12 feeds/day; on demand
  • Newborn loses ≤7% body weight in first week; should regain by 10–14 days
  • Latch: wide-open mouth, lower lip flanged out, areola in mouth, audible swallowing
  • Adequate intake: 6+ wet diapers/day by day 4; yellow seedy stools

Formula feeding: iron-fortified formula; 2–3 oz every 3–4 hr initially.

Vitamin D 400 IU/day for all breastfed infants from birth.

Injury Prevention

Safe sleep (SIDS prevention):

  • "Back to sleep" — supine on firm mattress
  • No soft bedding, pillows, blankets, stuffed animals, bumpers
  • Room-share without bed-share
  • Avoid overheating (light blanket, swaddling per safe-sleep guidelines)
  • Pacifier at sleep may reduce SIDS

Other safety:

  • Rear-facing car seat in back seat for every ride home from hospital
  • Never leave on elevated surfaces unattended
  • Always support head and neck
  • Hand hygiene; limit exposure to ill visitors
  • No smoking around newborn
  • Bathwater temp ≤ 100°F; never leave unattended near water
  • CPR training recommended for caregivers
Worked Example Fetal Growth & Development by Trimester Ch 3 — Maternal Adaptation in Early Pregnancy
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Developmental Stage
Fetal Period — Conception through Birth (~40 weeks)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 3 — Maternal Adaptation in Early Pregnancy
Expected Growth and Development

Physical Development

1st trimester (0–13 wk):

  • Weeks 3–8: embryonic period — all major organ systems form (organogenesis); most vulnerable to teratogens
  • Week 9: fetal period begins; sex differentiation
  • By 12 weeks: heart fully formed, kidneys produce urine, head ≈ ½ length

2nd trimester (14–27 wk):

  • Rapid linear growth; lanugo, vernix, fingernails
  • 16–20 weeks: quickening (maternal awareness of movement)
  • ~24 weeks: viability threshold

3rd trimester (28–40 wk):

  • Subcutaneous fat deposition
  • Surfactant production matures (L/S ratio 2:1 = lung maturity)
  • Settles head-down (vertex) by ~36 weeks

Cognitive Development

Brain and nervous system develop rapidly throughout gestation:

  • Neural tube closes weeks 3–4 — folic-acid-sensitive window
  • Brain growth continues through birth and beyond
  • Hearing develops at 24–28 weeks — fetus responds to maternal voice and external sound
  • Sleep-wake cycles emerge in the 3rd trimester
  • Habituation (decreased response to repeated stimuli) is measurable late in pregnancy

Psychosocial Development

  • Fetal movement patterns become organized by mid-pregnancy
  • Quickening enhances maternal-fetal attachment
  • Fetus responds to maternal heart rate, voice, and stress hormones
  • 3rd-trimester kick counts are a daily fetal-wellbeing check
  • Foundation for postnatal attachment laid prenatally

Age-Appropriate Activities

  • Avoidance of teratogens — alcohol, tobacco, recreational drugs, category D/X meds
  • Maternal moderate exercise supports fetal oxygenation
  • Left-lateral position optimizes placental perfusion
  • Talking, reading, and music exposure (auditory stimulation)
  • Kick counts daily in the 3rd trimester

Health Promotion

Optimal fetal outcomes depend on consistent prenatal care, maternal nutrition, teratogen avoidance, stress reduction, and timely identification of risk factors. Anticipatory guidance addresses both maternal and fetal needs at each visit.

Immunizations

  • Tdap each pregnancy, ideally 27–36 weeks (passive immunity to newborn against pertussis)
  • Influenza any trimester
  • COVID-19 boosters as recommended
  • RhoGAM at 28 weeks if Rh-negative
  • Avoid live vaccines: MMR, varicella, live influenza

Health Screening

1st trimester: dating ultrasound; nuchal translucency 11–13 wk; first-trimester serum screen.

2nd trimester: MSAFP or Quad marker 15–20 wk; anatomy ultrasound 18–20 wk; amniocentesis if indicated.

3rd trimester: growth ultrasound; NST, BPP, kick counts; GBS rectovaginal swab 35–37 wk.

Nutrition

  • +300–500 kcal/day above prepregnancy (2nd–3rd trimester)
  • Folic acid 600 mcg/day — neural tube
  • Iron 27 mg/day — fetal stores
  • Calcium 1000 mg/day · DHA/omega-3 for brain development
  • Avoid: alcohol (FAS), high-mercury fish (CNS injury), unpasteurized dairy/deli meats (listeria), excessive caffeine (>200 mg/day)

Injury Prevention

  • Teratogen avoidance — alcohol, tobacco, illicit drugs, isotretinoin, warfarin, ACE inhibitors
  • Seatbelt — lap belt below the pregnant abdomen, shoulder strap between the breasts
  • Avoid hot tubs/saunas (especially 1st trimester — neural-tube risk)
  • Avoid contact sports and high-fall-risk activity in 2nd–3rd trimester
  • Food safety against listeria, toxoplasmosis, salmonella
  • CMV exposure prevention (handwashing around young children)
Worked Example Maternal Physiologic Adaptation Across Pregnancy Ch 3 — Maternal Adaptation in Early Pregnancy
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Developmental Stage
Pregnancy (Conception through Birth)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 3 — Maternal Adaptation in Early Pregnancy
Expected Growth and Development

Physical Development

  • Reproductive: uterus 50 g → 1,000 g; cervix softens (violet-blue); ovulation/menses cease; baseline FHR 110–160
  • Cardiovascular: CO ↑ 30–50%; blood volume ↑ 30–45%; HR ↑ 10–15; S3 audible after 20 wk; murmurs possible
  • Respiratory: O₂ demand ↑; diaphragm elevated ~4 cm; SOB common in 3rd trimester
  • Musculoskeletal: relaxin softens joints → lordosis, back/leg discomfort, balance changes
  • GI: nausea, constipation, organs displaced upward
  • Renal: GFR ↑; urinary frequency; total urine unchanged
  • Endocrine: placenta (largest endocrine organ) produces hCG, progesterone, estrogen, hPL, prostaglandins

Cognitive Development

  • "Pregnancy brain" — mild memory/concentration changes
  • Hyperawareness of fetal movement and bodily change
  • Body image adjustment
  • Anticipatory thinking — parenting planning, role rehearsal

Psychosocial Development

Rubin's four maternal tasks across the pregnancy:

  1. Acceptance of the pregnancy and the changing body
  2. Identification with the maternal role — fantasy and role rehearsal
  3. Reordering of relationships — partner, family, friends, work
  4. Establishing relationship with the fetus — attachment foundation

Ambivalence early is normal; persistent dread or absence of attachment after the 2nd trimester warrants assessment.

Age-Appropriate Activities

  • Prenatal classes — childbirth education, breastfeeding, newborn care
  • Moderate exercise — walking, swimming, prenatal yoga, stationary bike
  • Avoid: contact sports, high-altitude exercise, scuba, hot yoga
  • Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises
  • Prenatal massage by trained provider

Health Promotion

Pregnancy is the highest-leverage period for primary prevention — establishing routines for nutrition, exercise, stress management, and safe practices benefits both the pregnant client and the fetus. Anticipatory guidance and family-centered support across all 4 of Rubin's tasks.

Immunizations

  • Tdap each pregnancy, 27–36 weeks (passive infant immunity to pertussis)
  • Influenza any trimester
  • COVID-19 boosters as recommended
  • Avoid live vaccines: MMR, varicella, live attenuated influenza, smallpox

Health Screening

1st trimester: initial labs (CBC, blood type, Rh, antibody screen, rubella titer, HBsAg, HIV, RPR/VDRL, GC/chlamydia, UA); dating ultrasound; NT scan.

2nd trimester: MSAFP/Quad marker 15–20 wk; anatomy ultrasound 18–20 wk; 1-hr GCT at 24–28 wk.

3rd trimester: GBS rectovaginal culture 35–37 wk; repeat HCT and antibody screen; growth ultrasound if indicated.

Nutrition

  • +300 kcal/day (2nd–3rd trimester) — not "eating for two"
  • Folic acid 600 mcg/day; iron 27 mg/day; calcium 1,000 mg/day
  • Weight gain per pre-pregnancy BMI (underweight 28–40 lb; normal 25–35 lb; overweight 15–25 lb; obese 11–20 lb)
  • Hydration; avoid alcohol, raw/undercooked foods, high-mercury fish, unpasteurized dairy, deli meats
  • Limit caffeine to <200 mg/day

Injury Prevention

  • Seatbelt — lap below pregnant belly, shoulder between breasts
  • Fall prevention — center-of-gravity shifts; nonslip footwear; avoid step-ups
  • Avoid hot tubs/saunas (1st trimester especially)
  • Avoid heavy lifting (> 15 lb after 2nd trimester) and prolonged standing
  • IPV screening — pregnancy is a high-risk period for intimate partner violence
  • Avoid teratogens (alcohol, tobacco, illicit drugs, certain meds)
Worked Example Postpartum Maternal Adaptation (Body Systems) Ch 17 — Postpartum Physiologic Changes
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Developmental Stage
Postpartum — Birth through ~6 Weeks (Puerperium)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 17 — Postpartum Physiologic Changes
Expected Growth and Development

Physical Development

  • Uterus: involution 1,000 g → 60–80 g by 6 wk; fundus descends ~1 cm/day; afterpains (more with multips and breastfeeding)
  • Lochia: rubra (d 1–3 dark red) → serosa (d 4–10 pinkish-brown) → alba (d 10–8 wk yellow-white)
  • Perineum: edema/bruising; episiotomy/laceration healing 2–3 weeks (complete 4–6 mo)
  • Breasts: colostrum → mature milk transition in 3–5 days ("milk coming in"); engorgement
  • Cardiovascular: diuresis/diaphoresis days 2–5; weight loss ~19 lb in 5 days; hypercoagulable state (DVT risk)
  • GI/GU: normal voiding pattern restored; constipation common; perineum tenderness affects defecation
  • Hematologic: WBC may rise 25,000–30,000 (not infection by itself)

Cognitive Development

  • Sleep deprivation dominant influence on cognition
  • Postpartum mood spectrum: blues (50–80%, self-limited <2 wk) vs depression (10–15%) vs psychosis (<0.2%, psychiatric emergency)
  • Cognitive recovery as sleep stabilizes; persistent impairment warrants screening for depression/anxiety/thyroid

Psychosocial Development

Rubin's postpartum phases:

  1. Taking-in (1–2 days) — passive, dependent, reflective; need for nurturing
  2. Taking-hold (2–10 days) — active, learning, may feel anxious about competence
  3. Letting-go (after day 10) — role acceptance, autonomy, family reorganization

Maternal role attainment continues for ~4 months as the new mother integrates the role.

Screen for postpartum mood disorders at 2-week and 6-week visits.

Age-Appropriate Activities

  • Early ambulation — DVT prevention
  • Kegel (pelvic-floor) exercises — start postpartum day 1 if comfortable
  • Graduated return to exercise; no high-impact for 4–6 weeks
  • Rest with the newborn's sleep cycle
  • Pelvic-rest until 6-week visit (no intercourse, tampons, douching until lochia stops and provider clears)

Health Promotion

The 6-week postpartum visit is the anchor for maternal recovery, contraception planning, mental-health screening, and follow-up of any pregnancy complications (GDM, hypertension, postpartum thyroiditis).

Immunizations

  • Rubella/MMR if nonimmune or low titer — given postpartum (cannot give during pregnancy); avoid pregnancy ×28 days after
  • Varicella if susceptible — same caution
  • Tdap if not given prenatally
  • RhoGAM IM within 72 hr if Rh-negative with Rh-positive newborn
  • If receiving both live vaccine AND RhoGAM → test Rh antibody titer at 3 months

Health Screening

  • Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) at 2-week and 6-week visits
  • Blood pressure follow-up if hypertensive disorder in pregnancy
  • 2-hr OGTT at 6–12 weeks postpartum if GDM (screens for residual type 2 DM)
  • Thyroid testing if symptoms (postpartum thyroiditis)
  • Lochia, fundal involution, and incision/perineal healing checks

Nutrition

  • Lactating: +330–400 kcal/day first 6 mo; +400–500 kcal/day after 6 mo; +1,000 mL fluid/day
  • Non-lactating: gradual return to pre-pregnancy needs
  • Continue prenatal vitamin while breastfeeding
  • Iron repletion if significant blood loss
  • Avoid alcohol if lactating (or pump-and-dump 2–3 hr per drink)

Injury Prevention

  • DVT prevention — early ambulation, hydration, leg exercises
  • PPH red flags — saturating a perineal pad in <1 hour, passing large clots, dizziness with standing
  • Perineal/wound care; sitz baths; ice pack first 24 hr
  • Fall risk with weakness, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension
  • Lift baby properly (avoid back injury)
  • Newborn safe sleep education (SIDS reduction)
Worked Example Preterm vs Term Newborn Maturity Ch 27 — Management of Newborn Complications
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Developmental Stage
Newborn — Gestational Age Classification (preterm < 37 wk vs term 37–42 wk)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 27 — Management of Newborn Complications
Expected Growth and Development

Physical Development

Gestational age is scored with the Ballard (Dubowitz) assessment (neuromuscular + physical maturity), ideally within 48 hr.

Preterm (< 37 wk) findings:

  • Minimal subcutaneous fat; head large relative to body; small fontanels; soft skull and rib cage
  • Abundant lanugo (back, forearms, face); few or no sole creases
  • Weak grasp; eyes may be fused if 22–24 wk
  • Periodic breathing (5–10 sec pauses) is normal; apnea ≥ 20 sec is not

Term (37–42 wk) findings: ample subcutaneous fat, sole creases over the whole foot, firm skull, descended testes/labia covering clitoris, strong reflexes.

Classification: AGA 10–90%ile · SGA <10%ile · LGA >90%ile or >4000 g · LBW ≤2500 g.

Cognitive Development

Neurologic maturity parallels gestational age:

  • Preterm reflexes (suck, swallow, gag, grasp) are weak or absent — a coordinated suck-swallow-breathe develops ~32–34 weeks
  • Intact gag plus suck/swallow is required before oral feeding (aspiration risk)
  • Sleep-wake organization and habituation are immature in preterm newborns
  • Term newborns show organized states and reliable reflexes (Moro, rooting, tonic neck, Babinski)

Psychosocial Development

  • Preterm newborns tolerate limited stimulation — cluster care, smooth/light touch, quiet low-light environment
  • Support parent-infant attachment despite NICU separation (skin-to-skin/kangaroo care when stable)
  • Non-nutritive sucking (pacifier during gavage) is soothing and supports later feeding
  • Term newborns engage in en face, quiet-alert bonding within the first hour

Age-Appropriate Activities

  • Kangaroo (skin-to-skin) care once thermally and cardiopulmonary stable
  • Non-nutritive sucking; containment/swaddling for self-regulation
  • Minimal handling and clustered care to conserve energy/oxygen
  • Developmental positioning (flexed, midline) to mimic intrauterine posture

Health Promotion

The preterm newborn's priorities are thermoregulation, respiratory support, and safe nutrition. Anticipatory guidance prepares parents for prolonged hospitalization, feeding readiness cues, and follow-up for long-term complications.

Immunizations

  • Immunize by chronological age (not corrected age), at the usual schedule
  • Hepatitis B may be deferred until the newborn is ≥ 2,000 g or 1 month old (if mother HBsAg-negative)
  • RSV prophylaxis (palivizumab/nirsevimab) for eligible preterm infants in RSV season
  • Ensure household/caregivers are up to date (cocooning)

Health Screening

  • Ballard for gestational age; serial weight, length, head circumference on growth curves
  • Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) eye exams; hearing screen
  • Newborn metabolic screen; glucose and bilirubin monitoring (higher risk)
  • Periodic head ultrasound for intraventricular hemorrhage if very preterm

Nutrition

  • Verify gag + suck/swallow before any oral feeding; otherwise gavage or parenteral nutrition (most < 34 wk)
  • Fortified breast milk/preterm formula for higher calorie, protein, calcium, phosphorus
  • Monitor I&O and daily weight; pacifier for non-nutritive sucking during gavage
  • Advance feeds slowly; watch for feeding intolerance (a hypothermia/NEC sign)

Injury Prevention

  • Thermoregulation via radiant warmer/isolette — hypothermia causes apnea, cyanosis, hypoglycemia
  • Monitor for bleeding from puncture sites; strict aseptic technique (infection risk)
  • Surfactant and oxygen as prescribed; assess for respiratory distress (flaring, retractions, grunting)
  • Safe-sleep teaching for discharge; car-seat tolerance screening before discharge
Worked Example Infant Reflexes & Neuromotor Development Ch 23 — Newborn Assessment
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Developmental Stage
Newborn — Primitive Reflexes (birth to ~1 year)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 23 — Newborn Assessment
Expected Growth and Development

Physical Development

Eight primitive reflexes — elicit and document presence, symmetry, and persistence:

  • Sucking & rooting — stroke cheek/mouth → head turns and sucks (fades 3–4 mo, up to 1 yr)
  • Palmar grasp — finger in palm → fingers curl (lessens by 3–4 mo)
  • Plantar grasp — finger at base of toes → toes curl down (birth to 8 mo)
  • Moro (startle) — head/trunk drop to ≥ 30° → symmetric arm extension/abduction, fingers form a "C" (absent by 6 mo)
  • Tonic neck (fencer) — turn head to one side → same-side arm/leg extend, opposite flex (birth to 3–4 mo)
  • Babinski — stroke outer sole upward → toes fan up/out (birth to 1 yr)
  • Stepping — hold upright, feet on surface → stepping movements (birth to 4 wk)
  • Galant (trunk incurvation) — stroke alongside spine → trunk curves toward the stroked side

Cognitive Development

Reflexes are the earliest measure of central nervous system integrity:

  • Symmetry matters — an asymmetric Moro or absent grasp suggests injury (e.g., brachial plexus/Erb palsy) or fracture
  • Reflexes should disappear on schedule; persistence beyond the expected age can signal a neurologic problem
  • Piaget: newborn is in the sensorimotor stage — behavior is reflexive, evolving toward intentional movement

Psychosocial Development

  • Rooting/sucking support feeding and early bonding (breast/bottle cues)
  • Grasp reflex encourages parent-infant hand-holding and attachment
  • Eliciting reflexes is a chance to teach parents normal newborn behavior and reduce anxiety
  • Consistent, gentle handling builds the infant's sense of security (trust vs mistrust)

Age-Appropriate Activities

  • Skin-to-skin and feeding cue responsiveness (rooting)
  • Talking, singing, high-contrast visual stimulation for the quiet-alert state
  • Tummy time while awake/supervised to build neck/trunk control
  • Swaddling for self-regulation; respond promptly to cues

Health Promotion

Reflex assessment is a core part of every newborn neurologic exam. Document each reflex's presence and symmetry, teach parents which behaviors are normal, and flag asymmetry or off-schedule persistence for follow-up.

Immunizations

  • Hepatitis B vaccine before discharge (routine newborn schedule)
  • Reflex/neuro screening does not change the immunization timeline
  • Reinforce the well-child visit schedule where development is rechecked

Health Screening

  • Full neurologic exam including all 8 reflexes for symmetry and strength
  • Ortolani/Barlow for developmental dysplasia of the hip
  • Newborn metabolic screen, hearing screen, and CCHD pulse oximetry
  • Re-evaluate reflex persistence at well-child visits

Nutrition

  • Intact rooting, suck, and swallow are prerequisites for safe oral feeding
  • A weak or absent suck warrants feeding evaluation (preterm/neurologic concern)
  • Feed on early cues (rooting, hand-to-mouth) rather than waiting for crying

Injury Prevention

  • Support the head/neck — newborn head control is immature
  • An exaggerated Moro can startle the infant; handle smoothly and support the back
  • Never shake an infant — teach coping with crying (shaken baby prevention)
  • Asymmetric reflexes → evaluate for clavicle fracture or brachial plexus injury
Worked Example Postmature (Post-term) Newborn Ch 27 — Management of Newborn Complications
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Developmental Stage
Newborn — Post-term (born after completion of 42 weeks)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 27 — Management of Newborn Complications
Expected Growth and Development

Physical Development

Postmature = born after 42 completed weeks. Two patterns depending on placental function:

  • Dysmaturity (placental degeneration): uteroplacental insufficiency → chronic hypoxia; newborn may be SGA
  • Continued growth (placenta still functioning): newborn becomes LGA → difficult delivery, cephalopelvic disproportion

Classic physical findings:

  • Wasted, thin appearance with loose skin and lost subcutaneous fat
  • Peeling, cracked, dry, leathery skin (decreased vernix)
  • Long fingernails and abundant hair; meconium-stained skin/cord/nails

Cognitive Development

Neurologic outcome depends on the degree of in-utero hypoxia:

  • Chronic hypoxia and perinatal asphyxia raise the risk of seizures and neurologic injury
  • Assess reflexes and tone closely — hypoglycemia and asphyxia can blunt responses
  • Most newborns without significant hypoxic injury follow normal neurodevelopment

Psychosocial Development

  • NICU-level monitoring may delay routine bonding — facilitate parental contact when stable
  • Educate parents that the wasted/peeling skin appearance is expected and improves
  • Support attachment during glucose/respiratory stabilization
  • Involve parents in cue-based care and feeding as the newborn stabilizes

Age-Appropriate Activities

  • Skin-to-skin once thermally and cardiopulmonary stable
  • Cue-based feeding to correct hypoglycemia
  • Gentle skin care/emollient for the dry, cracked skin
  • Minimal cold exposure — prompt drying and warming

Health Promotion

Postmature newborns are at high risk for meconium aspiration, hypoglycemia, polycythemia, and cold stress. Priorities are airway/respiratory support, glucose stabilization, and thermoregulation, with close monitoring for persistent pulmonary hypertension.

Immunizations

  • Routine newborn hepatitis B before discharge once stable
  • Immunize by chronological age on the standard schedule
  • Ensure follow-up well-child visits for ongoing monitoring

Health Screening

  • Blood glucose monitoring (high hypoglycemia risk from depleted glycogen)
  • Hematocrit for polycythemia; bilirubin monitoring
  • Respiratory assessment for meconium aspiration and persistent pulmonary hypertension
  • Temperature monitoring for cold stress

Nutrition

  • Early, frequent feeding to correct/prevent hypoglycemia
  • Monitor blood glucose before feeds per protocol; IV dextrose if symptomatic
  • Monitor I&O and daily weight; the wasted newborn has poor energy reserves

Injury Prevention

  • Anticipate meconium aspiration — have resuscitation ready at delivery
  • LGA postmature → watch for birth trauma (clavicle fracture, Erb palsy) and asphyxia
  • Thermoregulation with radiant warmer; prevent cold stress
  • Skin protection for the fragile, cracked, peeling skin
ATI Active Learning Template

Medication

Active · 18 examples
Worked Example Methotrexate (Trexall) Ch 7 — Bleeding During Pregnancy · Ectopic Pregnancy
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Methotrexate (Trexall)
Category Class
Antineoplastic — Folic Acid Antagonist
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Bleeding During Pregnancy
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking DNA synthesis and stopping cell division. In ectopic pregnancy, dissolves the trophoblast tissue.

Therapeutic Use

  • Termination of unruptured ectopic pregnancy
  • Preserves fertility (vs surgical tube removal)
  • Also used: rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, certain cancers

Complications

  • Bone marrow suppression (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia)
  • GI ulcers, mouth sores
  • Hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity
  • Photosensitivity
  • Tubal rupture (despite treatment)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Confirmed/desired pregnancy (Category X)
  • Breastfeeding
  • Hepatic or renal disease
  • Peptic ulcer disease
  • Immunodeficiency

Interactions

  • Folic acid (decreases efficacy — avoid prenatals)
  • NSAIDs — increase methotrexate toxicity
  • Penicillins — increase toxicity
  • Alcohol — hepatotoxicity

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Serial declining hCG (weekly until negative)
  • No tubal rupture signs
  • Fallopian tube preserved on follow-up
  • Resumption of normal menses

Medication Administration

  • IM injection (single-dose protocol most common)
  • Verify pregnancy is unruptured before administration
  • Baseline labs: CBC, hepatic, renal panels
  • Pre-treatment hCG to establish baseline

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor hCG levels post-treatment (weekly)
  • Assess for tubal rupture: severe pain, hypotension, shoulder pain
  • Monitor CBC, hepatic, renal labs
  • Assess for bleeding, infection signs
  • Emotional support; pregnancy-loss resources

Client Education

  • Avoid folic-acid–containing vitamins — toxic response prevention
  • Use sun protection (photosensitivity)
  • No alcohol during therapy
  • Report severe abdominal/shoulder pain immediately (rupture)
  • Avoid pregnancy × 3 months after treatment
  • Possible side effects: nausea, fatigue, mouth sores
  • Use reliable contraception during follow-up
Worked Example Betamethasone (Celestone) Ch 7 — Bleeding During Pregnancy · Placenta Previa
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Betamethasone (Celestone)
Category Class
Glucocorticoid / Corticosteroid
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Bleeding During Pregnancy
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Crosses placenta and stimulates surfactant production by fetal alveolar Type II cells. Reduces incidence of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), intraventricular hemorrhage, and necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm neonates.

Therapeutic Use

  • Promote fetal lung maturity in anticipated preterm delivery (24–34 wks)
  • Used in placenta previa with active bleeding requiring early delivery
  • Also: preterm labor, PPROM, abruption

Complications

  • Maternal: hyperglycemia, hypertension, transient leukocytosis
  • Pulmonary edema (with concurrent tocolytics)
  • Infection masking
  • Fetal: minimal short-term; potential adrenal suppression

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Active maternal infection
  • Gestational diabetes (glucose monitoring required)
  • Poorly controlled hypertension
  • Systemic fungal infection

Interactions

  • Tocolytics — combined risk of pulmonary edema
  • Antidiabetic agents — glucose elevation
  • NSAIDs — GI bleeding risk
  • Live vaccines — avoid

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Both doses completed (24h apart)
  • Reduced neonatal RDS if preterm delivery occurs
  • Optimal benefit 24h after first dose
  • Continued benefit ~7 days post-completion

Medication Administration

  • 12 mg IM × 2 doses, 24 hours apart
  • Deep IM injection (gluteal)
  • Document doses given and timing
  • Optimal benefit within 24–48 hours of first dose

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor maternal blood glucose (especially diabetic)
  • Assess maternal fundal height, FHR
  • Watch for pulmonary edema if tocolytics co-administered
  • Monitor temperature for infection signs
  • Document fetal movements

Client Education

  • Purpose: help baby's lungs mature in case of early delivery
  • Monitor blood glucose if diabetic; insulin may need adjustment
  • Both doses needed for full effect — return for second dose in 24h
  • Continue prescribed bed rest / activity restrictions
  • Report any fever, increased contractions, or fluid leakage
Worked Example Rho(D) Immune Globulin (RhoGAM) Ch 7 — Bleeding During Pregnancy · Universal Rh-negative
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Rho(D) Immune Globulin (RhoGAM)
Category Class
Immune Globulin
Review Module Chapter
Ch 7 — Bleeding During Pregnancy
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Provides passive anti-D IgG antibodies that destroy any fetal Rh-positive RBCs in maternal circulation BEFORE the maternal immune system produces its own anti-D antibodies. Prevents future Rh isoimmunization.

Therapeutic Use

  • Routine at 28 weeks gestation for Rh-negative mothers
  • Within 72 hours postpartum if baby is Rh-positive
  • After spontaneous abortion, ectopic, abruption, GTD
  • Amniocentesis, CVS, abdominal trauma

Complications

  • Local reactions (injection site pain, swelling)
  • Fever, chills
  • Hypersensitivity (rare)
  • Hemolysis if given to Rh+ patient — DO NOT give

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Rh-positive mother — no benefit, risk of hemolysis
  • Known hypersensitivity to immune globulin
  • IgA deficiency — anaphylaxis risk
  • Maternal already sensitized (positive Coombs)

Interactions

  • Live vaccines — avoid 3 months post-administration (decreased response)
  • Other immune globulins — no clinically significant interaction

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • Indirect Coombs negative on follow-up
  • No anti-D antibodies developed
  • No Rh sensitization in future pregnancies

Medication Administration

  • IM injection (gluteal muscle)
  • Standard dose 300 mcg for full-term events
  • Lower doses (50 mcg) for early pregnancy losses (< 13 wks)
  • Within 72 hours of qualifying event
  • Document type, lot number, dose

Nursing Interventions

  • Verify Rh status: mother Rh-negative, baby/POC Rh-positive
  • Confirm indirect Coombs negative pre-administration
  • Monitor for hypersensitivity reaction × 30 min post-injection
  • Document administration and rationale

Client Education

  • Why given: prevent your body from making antibodies that could harm a future baby
  • Always inform future providers of Rh status
  • May feel mild soreness at injection site
  • Carry RhoGAM card; show to all healthcare providers
  • Future pregnancies will require Rh testing and possible repeat injections
  • Avoid live vaccines × 3 months after dose
Worked Example Combined Oral Contraceptives (COCs) Ch 1 — Contraception · Hormonal methods
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Combined Oral Contraceptives (estrogen + progestin)
Category Class
Hormonal contraceptive
Review Module Chapter
Ch 1 — Contraception
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Estrogen + progestin combination suppresses ovulation by inhibiting the hypothalamic GnRH and pituitary LH/FSH release. Thickens cervical mucus to block sperm. Alters the uterine decidua to prevent implantation.

Therapeutic Use

  • Contraception (primary)
  • Decreases menstrual blood loss & iron-deficiency anemia
  • Regulates irregular cycles, treats dysmenorrhea/menorrhagia
  • Acne improvement
  • Reduces functional ovarian cysts
  • Protects against endometrial, ovarian, and colon cancer

Complications

  • Venous thromboembolism (VTE) — DVT, PE; most serious risk, especially in smokers > 35, obese, family history of clotting disorders
  • Stroke and MI — risk substantially elevated in smokers over 35
  • Hypertension (monitor BP at follow-up)
  • Migraine — especially migraine with aura (CONTRAINDICATION due to stroke risk)
  • Cholestasis, gallbladder disease, benign hepatic adenomas
  • Breakthrough bleeding (common in first 3 months)
  • Nausea, breast tenderness, headaches (often resolve with continued use)
  • Weight changes
  • Mood changes, depression
  • ↓ libido
  • Melasma (skin pigmentation, worsened by sun)
  • Hypertriglyceridemia
  • Slight ↑ cervical cancer risk; ↑ breast cancer risk while taking (returns to baseline after stopping)
  • Decreased risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer (protective effect)

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Thromboembolic history, stroke, MI, CAD
  • Gallbladder/liver disease, liver tumor
  • Severe headache with focal neuro signs
  • Uncontrolled HTN, DM with vascular involvement
  • Estrogen-dependent cancer (current or past)
  • Pregnancy, lactating < 6 weeks postpartum
  • Smoker > 35 yo (increased thromboembolic risk)
  • Bariatric surgery, severe cirrhosis, lupus

Interactions

  • Anticonvulsants (decrease efficacy via liver enzyme induction)
  • Antifungals (rifampin notably)
  • Some antibiotics
  • Smoking magnifies cardiovascular risks

Evaluation of Medication Effectiveness

  • No pregnancy (regular menses returns during inactive pill week)
  • Tolerability: minimal adverse effects
  • Therapeutic benefit: cycle regulation, decreased dysmenorrhea
  • BP & weight stable on follow-up visits

Medication Administration

  • Oral, same time daily for consistency
  • Take at bedtime if nausea is an issue
  • Routine Pap and breast exam follow-up

Nursing Interventions

  • Screen for contraindications (smoking history, BP, DVT/MI history, age)
  • Baseline BP, weight
  • Educate on missed-dose protocol
  • Monitor for complications at each visit
  • Reinforce dual barrier method needed for STI protection

Client Education

  • Take at the same time each day
  • Report ACHES symptoms immediately: Abdominal pain · Chest pain/SOB · Headache (severe) · Eye changes · Severe leg pain
  • Missed dose: 1 pill → take ASAP. 2–3 pills → follow manufacturer instructions; use backup method until regular dosing resumes
  • No STI protection — use condom for STI prevention
  • Notify provider if surgery is planned (stop 4 weeks before to reduce thrombosis risk)
  • Annual follow-up with Pap and breast exam
  • Avoid smoking
Worked Example Magnesium Sulfate Ch 9 — Medical Conditions · Highest-yield maternal med
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Medication
Magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄)
Review Module Chapter
Ch 9 — Medical Conditions
Purpose of Medication

Expected Pharmacological Action

Depresses CNS irritability; relaxes smooth muscles. Decreases the threshold for seizure activity, preventing eclamptic seizures. Mild peripheral vasodilation, modest BP reduction. Crosses the placenta — neonatal effects expected with peripartum use.

Therapeutic Use

  • Severe preeclampsia (seizure prophylaxis)
  • Eclampsia (active seizure treatment)
  • Preterm labor < 32 weeks (neuroprotection of preterm infant)

Complications

  • Magnesium toxicity: loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression, cardiac arrest
  • Hypotension, flushing, warmth, nausea, drowsiness, and blurred vision
  • Pulmonary edema risk, especially with fluid overload or concurrent tocolytics
  • Neonatal respiratory depression, hypotonia, or low Apgar if used near birth

Contraindications/Precautions

  • Active vaginal bleeding
  • Cervical dilation > 6 cm (when used as tocolytic)
  • Chorioamnionitis
  • Gestation > 34 weeks (for tocolytic indication)
  • Acute fetal distress
  • Myasthenia gravis
  • Renal failure / oliguria (drug excreted renally)
