Worked Example Maternal-Newborn Attachment Concept spans Ch 17 – 19 (Postpartum Adaptation, Baby-Friendly Care, Discharge Teaching)
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Maternal-Newborn Attachment

Defining Characteristics

The reciprocal, enduring, and selective emotional and physical connection between the mother (or primary caregiver) and the newborn. Manifests as en face positioning, eye contact, identification by name, comforting touch and voice, protective behaviors, and the mother's preference for her own infant over others. Develops along a continuum: bonding (immediate) → attachment (over weeks to months).

Antecedents

Conditions that must be in place for attachment to occur:

  • Anticipation and acceptance of the pregnancy
  • Prenatal bonding (felt fetal movement, ultrasound viewing, naming)
  • Healthy maternal mental and physical state
  • Adequate social support and absence of significant stressors
  • Opportunity for early skin-to-skin contact and proximity
  • Newborn able to respond (alert, healthy, capable of cuing)

Negative Consequences

Results from impaired antecedents:

  • Failure to thrive in the newborn
  • Misreading of newborn cues → inadequate response
  • Increased risk of neglect and child maltreatment
  • Impaired language and social development
  • Postpartum depression in mother (bidirectional risk)
  • Disorganized attachment patterns in childhood

Related Concepts

  • Bonding — immediate, unidirectional (parent → infant) emotional response within hours of birth
  • Claiming — parents identify the newborn as their own through naming, identifying family resemblances
  • Taking-in / Taking-hold / Letting-go phases of maternal adaptation
  • Paternal engrossment — father's intense preoccupation with newborn
  • Reciprocity — bidirectional cuing and response between parent and infant

Exemplars

  • Skin-to-skin contact in the delivery room within the first hour
  • Breastfeeding initiation within the first 30–60 minutes
  • En face positioning during feeding and quiet alert states
  • Calling the newborn by name; speaking in "parentese"
  • Rooming-in to facilitate proximity and cue recognition
  • Father stroking and exploring the newborn's features (engrossment)
Worked Example Tissue Perfusion · Fetal Oxygenation Concept spans Ch 6 (Fetal Well-Being) + Ch 13 (Fetal Assessment)
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Tissue Perfusion — Fetal Oxygenation Exemplar

Defining Characteristics

Adequate oxygen delivery to tissues via patent vascular supply and gas exchange. In the fetus, perfusion depends on maternal-to-placental-to-fetal oxygen transfer. Reflected in fetal heart rate variability and reactivity, biophysical profile findings, and ultimately by an Apgar score showing vigorous neonatal transition. Impaired fetal perfusion manifests as late or prolonged decelerations, decreased variability, decreased movement, and acidotic cord blood gases.

Antecedents

Conditions that must be in place for adequate fetal perfusion:

  • Patent maternal vascular circulation (normotensive, normovolemic)
  • Adequate uteroplacental blood flow (absence of supine hypotensive syndrome)
  • Functional placenta without infarction, abruption, or insufficiency
  • Intact umbilical cord without compression, prolapse, or true knot
  • Adequate maternal oxygenation and hemoglobin concentration
  • Normal fetal hemoglobin (HbF) for high O₂ affinity

Negative Consequences

Results from impaired antecedents:

  • Fetal hypoxemia → hypoxia → metabolic acidosis
  • Late decelerations on FHR monitoring (uteroplacental insufficiency)
  • Decreased fetal movement and tone
  • Low Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes
  • Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
  • Stillbirth or perinatal mortality

Related Concepts

  • Uteroplacental insufficiency — chronic compromise of placental perfusion
  • Cord compression — acute interruption of fetal blood flow
  • Fetal heart rate patterns — variability, accelerations, decelerations (VEAL CHOP)
  • Apgar scoring — neonatal transition assessment
  • Oxygenation, gas exchange, acid-base balance

Exemplars

  • Reactive NST (≥ 2 accelerations of 15 bpm × 15 sec in 20 min)
  • Biophysical profile (BPP) score of 8–10
  • Negative contraction stress test (no late decels with contractions)
  • Category I FHR tracing (baseline 110–160, moderate variability, no late/variable decels)
  • Vigorous newborn at delivery (Apgar ≥ 7 at 1 min, ≥ 9 at 5 min)
  • Normal cord gas pH (≥ 7.20) at birth
Worked Example Pain in Labor Concept spans Ch 12 (Pain Management in Labor), Ch 14 (Nursing Care of Labor)
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Pain in Labor

Defining Characteristics

A multi-source, stage-specific subjective pain experience unique to childbirth:

  • First stage — visceral pain: cervical dilation/effacement, uterine ischemia from contractions, distension of the lower uterine segment; felt as back and leg pain
  • Second stage — somatic pain: fetal descent, stretching of vagina/perineum, pelvic structure pressure, soft-tissue lacerations; burning, splitting, tearing
  • Third stage: similar to first-stage pain but rapidly resolving with placental delivery

Modulated by the fear-tension-pain cycle — anxiety ↑ muscle tension ↑ pain perception ↑ slowed labor progression.

Antecedents

  • Cervical dilation and effacement
  • Uterine contractions causing ischemia
  • Stretching of cervix, vagina, perineum
  • Fetal descent and pelvic-structure pressure
  • Fear, anxiety, prior trauma — amplify perception
  • Cultural beliefs and expectations about birth
  • Previous birth experience (positive or negative)
  • Sleep deprivation, exhaustion, dehydration

Negative Consequences

When inadequately managed:

  • Maternal exhaustion → labor dysfunction → operative delivery
  • Hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis → reduced placental perfusion → fetal compromise
  • Catecholamine release → uteroplacental vasoconstriction
  • Fear-tension-pain cycle → slowed labor → cascade of interventions
  • Traumatic birth experience → postpartum mood disorders, PTSD risk
  • Impaired early bonding and breastfeeding initiation

Related Concepts

Labor progression, fear-tension-pain cycle, somatic vs visceral pain, fetal-maternal oxygenation, regional anesthesia (epidural/spinal), nonpharmacological pain management, postpartum mood, birth trauma.

Exemplars

  • Positive (nonpharmacologic): client uses paced breathing, hydrotherapy, position changes, and continuous partner support; pain is tolerable, labor progresses
  • Positive (pharmacologic): epidural anesthesia placed after 4 cm dilation provides effective relief without significant maternal hypotension or fetal effect
  • Negative (untreated severe pain): client unable to cope → exhaustion → dysfunctional labor → operative delivery; postpartum reports of traumatic birth experience
  • Negative (cultural barriers unaddressed): client culturally expected to bear pain silently; nurse misses cues → underrecognized severe pain
Worked Example Lactation Concept spans Ch 17 (Postpartum Physiologic Changes), Ch 25 (Newborn Nutrition)
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Lactation

Defining Characteristics

The production, secretion, and ejection of milk from the mammary glands to nourish the newborn. Initiated by the hormonal shift at delivery (drop in placental estrogen/progesterone) and maintained by:

  • Prolactin — milk production (anterior pituitary)
  • Oxytocin — milk ejection / let-down reflex (posterior pituitary)

Milk progression: colostrum (concentrated, immunoglobulin-rich, days 0–3) → transitional milk → mature milk by days 3–5 ("milk coming in"). Production is demand-driven — emptying drives further production.

Antecedents

  • Breast development during pregnancy (ductal proliferation under hormonal influence)
  • Hormonal preparation: estrogen, progesterone, prolactin, hPL during pregnancy
  • Placental delivery → drop in inhibitory hormones → prolactin rises
  • Effective infant latch and suckling — provides the stimulus
  • Maternal nutrition and hydration (+330–400 kcal/day, +1,000 mL fluid/day)
  • Early skin-to-skin contact and frequent feedings (8–12 / 24 hr)
  • Absence of inhibitory factors (severe stress, certain meds, breast surgery)

Negative Consequences

When lactation is impaired or disrupted:

  • Engorgement → milk stasis → mastitis risk
  • Inadequate milk supply → infant failure to thrive, hyperbilirubinemia, hypoglycemia
  • Maternal frustration → early breastfeeding cessation
  • Loss of one major feeding-based bonding opportunity
  • Loss of the protective effects of breast milk on infant immunity, GI flora, and maternal cancer risk reduction
  • Cracked or bleeding nipples from poor latch → pain → further avoidance

Related Concepts

Maternal-newborn attachment, lactational amenorrhea, mastitis, breast engorgement, milk storage and pumping, formula feeding alternatives, breast self-exam.

Exemplars

  • Positive (effective lactation): deep latch with audible swallowing; 8–12 feedings per 24 hr; 6+ wet diapers and 3+ stools by day 4; mother reports comfortable feedings
  • Positive (anticipatory): early skin-to-skin within the first hour after birth; first feeding initiated in the delivery room
  • Negative (poor latch): pain with feeding (usually shallow latch); cracked nipples; infant fussy and inadequate weight gain → lactation consultant referral
  • Negative (suppression): client choosing not to breastfeed → tight-fitting bra, ice packs, avoid breast stimulation; let engorgement resolve naturally; do not express milk (perpetuates production)
  • Pharmacologic interference: pseudoephedrine and some hormonal contraceptives can reduce supply
Worked Example Postpartum Hemorrhage Concept spans Ch 14 (Labor Stages 3 & 4), Ch 17 (Postpartum), Ch 20 (Postpartum Hemorrhage & Complications)
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Postpartum Hemorrhage (Concept)

Defining Characteristics

Blood loss > 500 mL after vaginal birth OR > 1,000 mL after cesarean birth, with two end-organ endpoints: hypovolemic shock and anemia.

  • Early (primary) PPH — within the first 24 hours
  • Late (secondary) PPH — 24 hours to 6 weeks postpartum

Earliest indicator of hypovolemia: rising pulse and decreasing blood pressure — before visible distress.

Antecedents

Remembered as the "4 T's":

  • Tone (70–80%) — uterine atony (most common): retained placental fragments, prolonged or precipitous labor, oxytocin induction/augmentation, overdistension (multifetal, polyhydramnios, macrosomia), magnesium sulfate, anesthesia, operative delivery
  • Trauma — cervical, vaginal, or perineal lacerations; hematomas; uterine inversion or rupture
  • Tissue — retained placental fragments, subinvolution, placenta accreta/increta/percreta
  • Thrombin — coagulopathies (DIC, ITP, von Willebrand disease, severe preeclampsia/HELLP)

Negative Consequences

  • Hypovolemic shock → multi-organ failure → maternal death — PPH is a leading cause of maternal mortality globally
  • Severe anemia → fatigue, decreased lactation, prolonged recovery
  • Sheehan syndrome — postpartum pituitary necrosis from severe hypoperfusion → permanent panhypopituitarism
  • Hysterectomy as life-saving measure when uncontrolled
  • Increased risk of placenta accreta in future pregnancies (especially with prior cesarean + uterine instrumentation)
  • Birth trauma and impaired bonding

Related Concepts

Uterine atony, lochia (especially abnormal patterns), fundal massage, uterotonics (oxytocin, methylergonovine, carboprost, misoprostol), hypovolemic shock, DIC, retained placenta, placenta accreta, postpartum infection.

Exemplars

  • Tone exemplar: postpartum client with boggy fundus and heavy lochia → fundal massage (firms uterus), IV oxytocin, assess for retained tissue, empty bladder
  • Trauma exemplar: firm fundus but continuous bright-red bleeding → evaluate for genital-tract lacerations; expanding hematoma → unexplained pain + hemodynamic instability
  • Tissue exemplar: blood clots larger than a quarter, return to earlier lochia stage → retained placenta → manual exploration or D&C
  • Thrombin exemplar: oozing from IV sites, gums, surgical incisions without clotting → coagulopathy workup (DIC labs: PT/PTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer)
Worked Example Family Adaptation to Childbearing Concept spans Ch 18 (Maternal & Family Adaptation), Ch 19 (Postpartum Discharge Teaching), Ch 22 (Postpartum Mood Disorders)
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Family Adaptation to Childbearing

Defining Characteristics

The bidirectional adjustment of all family members to the addition of a new baby — distinct from the dyadic maternal-newborn attachment concept. Spans pregnancy through approximately one year postpartum and includes:

  • Maternal role attainment (Rubin/Mercer)
  • Co-parent/paternal adaptation
  • Sibling adaptation
  • Extended family role shifts
  • Renegotiation of the partnership/marriage

Antecedents

  • Pregnancy planning and acceptance by all family members
  • Existing role flexibility within the family
  • Couple/co-parent relationship quality before the pregnancy
  • Social and economic support; community connection
  • Cultural context and expectations regarding gender roles, extended family involvement
  • Sibling preparation and inclusion (if applicable)
  • Healthy maternal mental health throughout pregnancy and postpartum
  • Absence of significant stressors (financial, housing, IPV, prior loss)

Negative Consequences

  • Co-parent feelings of exclusion or displacement → emotional distance, relationship strain
  • Sibling regression, jealousy, or acting-out behaviors
  • Family conflict → impaired environment for infant care and attachment
  • Postpartum depression in the mother affects the entire family system; paternal/co-parent postpartum depression also occurs in ~10%
  • Intimate partner violence — pregnancy and the postpartum period are high-risk windows
  • Increased divorce/separation risk in the first year postpartum
  • Multigenerational impact when grandparental support is conflicted

Related Concepts

Maternal-newborn attachment, Rubin's maternal phases, paternal/co-parent adaptation, sibling adaptation, postpartum mood spectrum, family-centered care, intimate partner violence screening.

Exemplars

  • Positive (co-parent inclusion): partner attends prenatal visits, participates in labor and delivery, takes paternal leave; shares night feedings; reports growing into the role
  • Positive (sibling preparation): 4-year-old visits before discharge, gets a "big sister" gift from the baby; family meals continue; one-on-one time preserved
  • Negative (co-parent withdrawal): partner feels displaced when grandparent moves in to "help"; gradually emotionally distances → couple distress; needs validation and re-inclusion in care
  • Negative (sibling regression): previously toilet-trained 3-year-old has accidents and aggressive behavior toward the baby — normal regression, requires reassurance and inclusion rather than punishment
  • Negative (PPD impact): mother withdrawn and tearful; partner overwhelmed; older child senses tension — whole-family intervention with PPD treatment + practical and emotional support
Worked Example Thermoregulation Concept spans Ch 24 (Newborn Care) & Ch 27 (Newborn Complications)
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Thermoregulation

Defining Characteristics

The newborn's ability to balance heat production and heat loss to maintain a stable core temperature (axillary 36.5–37.5°C / 97.7–99.5°F). Newborns are vulnerable: large surface-area-to-weight ratio, blood vessels near the skin, minimal subcutaneous insulation, and an inability to shiver. They generate heat by metabolizing brown fat (nonshivering thermogenesis).

Antecedents

Conditions/factors that influence whether thermoregulation succeeds:

  • Adequate brown fat and glycogen stores (term gestation)
  • A warm delivery/care environment (ambient 22–26°C / 72–78°F)
  • Prompt drying and skin-to-skin/radiant warmth after birth
  • Control of the 4 heat-loss mechanisms: conduction, convection, evaporation, radiation
  • Intact skin and absence of asphyxia/sepsis

Negative Consequences

Cold stress sets off a dangerous cascade:

  • Cold stress → ↑ oxygen demand and rapid depletion of brown fat
  • Anaerobic metabolism → metabolic acidosis
  • Glucose consumed for heat → hypoglycemia
  • Pulmonary vasoconstriction → respiratory distress, hypoxia; can reopen fetal shunts (persistent pulmonary hypertension)
  • Manifestations: poor feeding, jitteriness, weak cry, lethargy, hypothermia, cyanosis/apnea

Related Concepts

  • Glucose regulation — cold stress drives hypoglycemia
  • Gas exchange / perfusion — hypothermia raises O₂ demand and impairs oxygenation
  • Acid-base balance — nonshivering thermogenesis can produce acidosis
  • Metabolism / nutrition — brown fat and glycogen fuel heat production

Exemplars

  • Conduction — preheat the radiant warmer, warm the stethoscope/scale, place newborn skin-to-skin on parent's chest
  • Convection — keep the bassinet out of fan/AC drafts, swaddle, keep the head covered
  • Evaporation — dry immediately after birth; delay the first bath until skin temp ≥ 36.5°C
  • Radiation — keep the crib away from cold windows/walls/outer surfaces
  • At-risk newborns: preterm, SGA/LGA, and infants of diabetic mothers
Worked Example Perinatal Infection & Immunity Concept spans Ch 8 (Maternal Infections), Ch 21 (Postpartum Infections) & Ch 27 (Neonatal Sepsis)
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Perinatal Infection & Immunity

Defining Characteristics

The body's defense against pathogens across the perinatal continuum, and the breakdown of that defense in the mother, postpartum client, or newborn. The newborn has an immature immune system and relies on passive immunity (transplacental IgG, IgA in colostrum/breast milk). Infection presents as maternal STIs/TORCH, postpartum endometritis/mastitis/wound infection, or neonatal sepsis.

Antecedents

Factors that raise infection risk perinatally:

  • PROM, prolonged labor, chorioamnionitis
  • Maternal STIs/TORCH, UTI, or substance use
  • Preterm birth and low birth weight (immature immunity)
  • Invasive procedures (internal monitoring, catheters, IV lines)
  • Cesarean birth, lacerations, retained products (postpartum)
  • Lack of breastfeeding (loss of passive immunity)

Negative Consequences

When defenses fail:

  • Neonatal sepsis — subtle, nonspecific signs: temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, apnea/grunting, hypo- or hyperglycemia, color changes
  • Untreated infection → septicemia, septic shock, meningitis, death
  • Maternal: endometritis, wound dehiscence, mastitis, progression to sepsis
  • Congenital/perinatal infection → long-term neuro/sensory impairment (TORCH)

Related Concepts

  • Thermoregulation — temperature instability is an early sepsis sign
  • Gas exchange / perfusion — sepsis causes apnea, desaturation, shock
  • Glucose regulation — hypo/hyperglycemia accompany sepsis
  • Nutrition — breast milk confers passive immunity (IgA)
  • Inflammation — the underlying host response

Exemplars

  • Maternal (Ch 8): GBS colonization → intrapartum penicillin; TORCH; HIV antiretroviral prophylaxis
  • Postpartum (Ch 21): endometritis (foul lochia, fever), mastitis, wound infection
  • Neonatal (Ch 27): sepsis neonatorum — common organisms GBS, E. coli, S. aureus/epidermidis, H. influenzae
  • Prevention: maternal screening, aseptic delivery, erythromycin eye prophylaxis, cord care, hand hygiene, breastfeeding
Worked Example Fluid & Electrolyte Balance Concept spans Ch 9 (Hyperemesis), Ch 17 (Postpartum Diuresis) & Ch 27 (Neonatal Glucose/Fluid)
Open chapter ↗
Student Name
Concept Analysis
Fluid & Electrolyte Balance

Defining Characteristics

The maintenance of adequate fluid volume and electrolyte concentration across the childbearing cycle. Pregnancy normally expands plasma volume; the perinatal period brings predictable fluid shifts (postpartum diuresis) and pathologic losses (vomiting, hemorrhage) that can tip the mother or newborn into dehydration or imbalance.

Antecedents

Conditions that challenge fluid/electrolyte homeostasis:

  • Hyperemesis gravidarum — persistent vomiting with weight loss
  • Postpartum blood loss and the normal mobilization of pregnancy fluid
  • Newborn's high body-water content and immature kidneys
  • Limited newborn glycogen/glucose reserves (preterm, SGA, IDM)
  • NPO status, oxytocin (antidiuretic effect), and labor exertion

Negative Consequences

When balance is lost:

  • Maternal hyperemesis → dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, ketonuria; fetal IUGR/SGA, preterm birth
  • Postpartum hemorrhage → hypovolemia and shock
  • Newborn → hypoglycemia, dehydration, weight loss > 10%, poor feeding
  • Oxytocin in large volumes of electrolyte-free fluid → water intoxication/hyponatremia

Related Concepts

  • Glucose regulation — newborn hypoglycemia overlaps fluid/feeding status
  • Perfusion — volume loss compromises maternal/fetal perfusion
  • Nutrition — intake drives hydration and electrolyte repletion
  • Thermoregulation — cold stress consumes glucose and fluid reserves
  • Acid-base balance — vomiting and ketosis alter pH

Exemplars

  • Hyperemesis (Ch 9): IV lactated Ringer's, antiemetics/pyridoxine, NPO then slow advance, monitor I&O and electrolytes
  • Postpartum (Ch 17): expected diuresis and diaphoresis clearing pregnancy fluid; monitor for hemorrhage
  • Newborn (Ch 27): early/frequent feeding and blood glucose monitoring; IV dextrose if symptomatic
  • Monitoring: daily weight, strict I&O, skin turgor/fontanel, mucous membranes, urine output
